newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Frustrated U.N. envoy leaves Zaire, EU team lands.
newsitem.headline: Frustrated U.N. envoy leaves Zaire, EU team lands.

text.p: U.N. special envoy Raymond Chretien left Zaire on Sunday after expressing his frustration at obstacles blocking efforts to save more than a million Hutu refugees and displaced Zaireans from death and disease.
"It's extremely frustrating for me to see more obstacles presenting themselves than possible solutions," he said on Saturday night after talks with the Zairean government.

"I have been given 10 days to report back to the (U.N.) Secretary General with a plan of action concentrating on the humanitarian question," he added, noting that the security of aid workers had to be guaranteed.
Zairean officials said that Chretien had left on Sunday as the European Union's outspoken aid commissioner, Emma Bonino, arrived for talks of her own. He left for Uganda and Rwanda.

Bonino, who has lambasted world indifference to the plight of the refugees, said before leaving Brussels that she was travelling to Zaire to get a first-hand account of the situation and wanted to visit refugee camps in war-ravaged eastern Zaire.

She said she was at a loss how to explain her mission to the refugees, who have been abandoned to their fate over a week after a Tutsi revolt there sent foreign aid workers fleeing to the comparative safety of neighbouring Rwanda and Burundi.
"God knows what I will tell them," Bonino said on Saturday. "How can I tell them the Security Council doesn't see...doesn't listen...doesn't care."
The Security Council on Saturday passed a resolution putting off any immediate prospect of a multinational force being deployed in eastern Zaire, where Tutsi rebels hold many of the main towns.
"The states who prevented a force being deployed are an international scandal...an international disgrace," Bonino said.

The European Commission wanted the council to call for the immediate creation of a multinational force. The United States -- mindful of its ill-fated involvement in a similar force in Somalia -- said it needed more time to study the options.
The council instead called on U.N. members to lay the groundwork for a multinational force but postponed a decision on deployment until November 20.
The crisis is rooted in Tutsi-Hutu hatred that has poisoned life for generations in neighbouring Rwanda and Burundi.
Hundreds of thousands of Rwandan Hutu refugees and displaced Zaireans fled the Tutsi revolt in the east. The whereabouts of many of them is unclear.
The Hutus fled Rwanda in 1994 fearing reprisals from returning Tutsi exiles after Hutu hardliners massacred up to a million minority Tutsis and their sympathisers.
Zaire accuses Tutsi-led Rwanda of fomenting the revolt to create a buffer zone between its border and armed Hutu hardliners living among the refugees.
Officials said Bonino began with talks with Zaire's interior, foreign and defence ministers and was due to meet part-Tutsi Prime Minister Kengo wa Dondo later.

Bonino backs the idea of a force to patrol so-called "aid corridors" so that relief can be given to the refugees. "We have the food for them. But we have to be able to get it to them. Every day, every hour is costing lives," she said in Brussels.
Chretien left Zaire after failing to persuade the government to back humanitarian corridors inside Zaire for the refugees.
Zaire backs the principle of an international force but says the refugees should be sent home and fed there.
